title: Truck Accidents
description: Truck accident claims usually involve more parties, faster evidence loss, and more complicated insurance and records questions than a standard car crash.
meta_title: Truck Accident Claims: Carriers, Logs and Evidence
main_html:
Truck Accidents

Educational only. Not legal advice. No endorsements or rankings.

Quick answer

A truck accident claim is usually harder than a car accident claim for three reasons, and none of them is about who hit whom. First, more than one company may be responsible: the driver, the motor carrier that employed or leased them, a maintenance contractor, the trailer's owner, and sometimes the broker or shipper who arranged the load. Second, the evidence that decides the case is mostly held by those companies rather than by the police report — electronic logs, engine data, inspection reports, dispatch messages, the driver's qualification file. Third, federal rules set how long a carrier has to keep each of those records, and some of those windows are measured in months, not years.

So the question that matters early is not how badly the vehicles were damaged. It is which records exist, who controls them, how long they survive, and whether anyone has asked for them to be preserved yet.

Who can be responsible besides the driver

Commercial trucking is organised in layers, and each layer is a possible defendant with its own insurance:

  • The motor carrier. A carrier is generally answerable for the negligence of a driver acting within the scope of their work, and separately for its own decisions — whom it hired, whether it checked their record, how it scheduled the route, whether it ignored earlier violations.
  • A leasing arrangement. Many drivers own their tractor and run under another company's authority. Federal leasing rules (49 CFR Part 376) are the reason "he was an independent contractor" is often not the end of the question.
  • Maintenance and repair vendors. If a brake, tyre or coupling failure contributed, whoever last serviced or inspected it may be in the picture.
  • Cargo and trailer parties. Shifted, overweight or badly secured loads point at whoever loaded and secured them, which is frequently not the driver.
  • Brokers and shippers. Less often, and depending heavily on the facts and the jurisdiction, the company that arranged or tendered the load.

This is also why total available insurance usually looks nothing like a private car claim. Interstate for-hire carriers must carry minimum coverage set by federal regulation (49 CFR 387.9), at levels well above the minimum a private driver carries, with higher floors again for certain hazardous cargo. Look the current figures up rather than trusting a number quoted in an advertisement.

The records that decide the case, and how long they last

Most interstate truck drivers have been required to record hours of service on an electronic logging device since the end of 2017, which means the driving day is usually documented in detail somewhere. The catch is retention. Under the hours-of-service rules (49 CFR 395.8), a carrier must keep records of duty status and their supporting documents for six months. Driver vehicle inspection reports (49 CFR 396.11) and annual inspection records (49 CFR 396.17 and 396.21) have their own, also finite, retention periods. Nothing obliges a company to keep them longer because someone might sue later.

Engine control module data — the "black box" figures for speed, braking and throttle in the seconds before impact — is more fragile still. It can be overwritten in normal operation or lost altogether when the tractor is repaired and put back on the road, which often happens within days.

  • Electronic logs and hours-of-service records, plus the fuel receipts, tolls and dispatch records that corroborate them.
  • Engine control module and telematics data, and any forward-facing or driver-facing camera footage.
  • Maintenance history, inspection reports and repair orders for the tractor and the trailer.
  • The driver qualification file (49 CFR 391.51): licence, medical certificate, prior employment checks, training.
  • Drug and alcohol testing records connected to the crash.
  • Bills of lading, weight tickets and load securement paperwork.

When to call a lawyer, and when to handle health first

Medical care comes first, always. But legal help tends to become urgent sooner in a truck case than in an ordinary collision, because the preservation clock is already running on records the reader cannot reach. The standard first step is a written preservation — or spoliation — letter to the carrier and its insurer, naming the specific records and data not to be destroyed, repaired over or recycled. Sent in the first weeks it is routine. Sent after six months it may be asking for something that is lawfully already gone.

If there is a serious or fatal injury, a commercial carrier involved, a disputed account of lane changes or braking, or any suggestion the truck was repaired quickly, this is not a case most people want to evaluate casually and late.

What you can check yourself, for free

The truck's door or bumper usually carries a USDOT number. The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration publishes a Company Snapshot for each one through its SAFER system: the legal and trading name, fleet size, driver count, the type of cargo carried, and the carrier's recent inspection and crash history. Photographing the USDOT number, the tractor and trailer plates and the trailer number at the scene, when it is safe to do so, is worth more later than any note about the weather.

  • Save every crash-scene photograph, truck identifier, trailer number and witness name you safely can.
  • Keep all correspondence from insurers, carriers, investigators and claims adjusters, and do not give a recorded statement before you understand what it is for.
  • Track medical care, work restrictions and lost time from the first day forward.
  • Ask early, in writing, what evidence should be preserved and which deadlines apply where you live.

Fees, costs, and what people misunderstand

Truck cases are usually still handled on a contingency fee, but the case costs behind that fee are heavier: reconstruction and trucking-standards experts, data downloads, depositions of corporate witnesses in other states, and a timeline that more often ends in litigation rather than an early settlement. Several defendants means several insurers, several sets of lawyers and more argument about which of them pays what share.

"Free consultation" tells a reader almost nothing about any of that. The questions that do are how case expenses are advanced and repaid, whether they come out before or after the fee percentage, what happens to them if the case is lost, and whether the firm has actually tried a case against a motor carrier or refers that work out.

Questions worth asking

A lawyer who does this work regularly should sound methodical rather than enthusiastic, and should be able to explain what makes truck evidence different before being asked.

  • What records matter most in a case like this, and have you sent a preservation letter yet?
  • Who might be responsible besides the driver, and how will you find out who they are?
  • How quickly can you get the engine data and the electronic logs, and what happens if they are already gone?
  • How are case expenses handled, and how do they interact with your fee?
  • What would make you think this case is stronger or weaker than it looks today?

Red flags and trust checks

Be wary if the intake conversation sounds identical to a basic auto claim, if nobody asks about the carrier, the trailer or the available records, if preservation is not mentioned at all, or if the marketing tone is louder than the legal explanation. Be wary too of a firm that promises a figure at intake: at that point nobody has seen the logs, the engine data or the medical course. In truck cases, confidence without process is not reassuring.

What to do next

Stabilise medical care. Preserve every identifier, photograph and document you already have, and write down what you remember while it is fresh. Look the carrier up on SAFER. Then compare lawyers on how they talk about carrier records, preservation and multiple defendants — and use the fee, evidence, red-flag and city pages here to pressure-test the shortlist before you commit to anyone.
